lessons.title: Basic evaluation of the couple
lessons.objective: Organise a simultaneous, stepwise, minimally invasive initial work-up of both partners, and know what not to order routinely.
lessons.closing: Three pillars from day one — ovulation, uterus and tubes, semen analysis — in both partners at once and without blame.

lessons.title: Age and fertility
lessons.objective: Explain that female age is the main predictor of fecundity, tell it apart from ovarian reserve, and place paternal age in context.
lessons.closing: Age guides the chance of pregnancy; reserve markers, the response to stimulation. Paternal age mainly raises questions about offspring.

lessons.title: When to evaluate: no delay with age
lessons.objective: Apply ASRM and NICE age and time thresholds for starting evaluation, and advise on the fertile window in the meantime.
lessons.closing: From 35–36 onwards the waiting time shortens; with a known cause, there is no wait. A loss while trying does not reset the clock.

items.title: Both partners, from day one
items.core: When a male partner contributes the sperm, evaluation of both partners should begin at the same time, with his reproductive history and at least one semen analysis from the outset. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
ASRM grounds this on the high prevalence of a contributing male factor. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]] The AUA/ASRM male guideline calls for concurrent assessment of both partners (Expert Opinion) and for one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level Grade B). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

NICE recommends seeing couples together, because both partners are affected by decisions on investigation and treatment (1.1.1), and offering both partners assessment after 1 year without pregnancy when there is no known or suspected cause (1.16.5). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

When donor sperm is needed (single women, female couples), ASRM advises a directed history, examination and laboratory evaluation as for any infertile patient, tailoring tubal and uterine assessment to history and risk. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.recall: At what point in the work-up is the male partner of a heterosexual couple with infertility evaluated?
items.pearl: Ordering the semen analysis at the first visit, rather than after her work-up is finished, is the practical way to apply simultaneous evaluation.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM 2021 (committee opinion). AUA/ASRM: concurrent evaluation = Expert Opinion; semen analysis = Strong, Grade B. NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would do: the three pillars of the basic work-up
items.core: The basic work-up includes ovulatory status, the structure and patency of the female reproductive tract, and semen analysis of the male partner. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
ASRM advises starting with the least invasive methods for the most common causes and tailoring pace and extent to the couple's preferences, age, duration of infertility and history. For ASRM, transvaginal ultrasound is the best imaging modality to assess uterine anatomy; HSG or sonohysterography are the recommended tests for tubal patency, and laparoscopy is not recommended routinely without suspected pelvic pathology or another indication. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

ESHRE considers HyCoSy and HSG valid tests for tubal patency (strong recommendation; ⊕⊕⊕○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NICE offers HSG to people without known comorbidities (such as PID, previous ectopic pregnancy or endometriosis) and laparoscopy and dye to those thought to have them (1.18.13, 1.18.15). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What are the three minimum components of the basic infertility work-up?

rows.text: Directed history and examination of both partners
Male partner: reproductive history + semen analysis
Laparoscopy: not routine without suspected pelvic pathology

visual.alt: Flow diagram: history and examination of both partners; then ovulation by menstrual history, uterus by transvaginal ultrasound, tubes by HSG or HyCoSy, and semen analysis. Note: laparoscopy is not routine without suspected pelvic pathology.

items.application: Use it as a minimum checklist at the first visit: if one of the three pillars is missing, the work-up is not yet complete.

items.title: Confirming ovulation with regular cycles: guidelines differ
items.core: With regular 21–35-day cycles, no additional test is needed to confirm ovulation unless there is hirsutism; a history of oligo- or amenorrhoea is enough to establish anovulation. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
ESHRE agrees in essence: with regular cycles, tests to confirm ovulation are not routinely recommended (good practice point); if confirmation is warranted, it states that tests such as urinary LH, ultrasound monitoring or mid-luteal progesterone can be used (conditional; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE differs: it reassures people with regular monthly cycles that they are likely ovulating (1.18.6), but offers mid-luteal serum progesterone even with regular cycles (1.18.7). It agrees on not using basal body temperature charts to confirm ovulation (1.18.9). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

If progesterone is measured, ASRM advises doing so about 1 week before expected menses, not on a fixed day such as day 21; a single value confirms ovulation but does not assess luteal phase quality. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.recall: With regular 28-day cycles and no hirsutism, is ovulation confirmation needed?
items.pearl: If you order progesterone, time it to the next expected period and do not use it to judge luteal phase “quality”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM 2021 and ESHRE 2023 (good practice point) versus NICE 2026: a genuine guideline discrepancy.

items.title: What I would not order routinely in the basic work-up
items.core: Without a clinical indication, ASRM does not recommend as part of the routine work-up: laparoscopy, advanced sperm function testing, postcoital testing, thrombophilia testing, immunological testing, karyotype, endometrial biopsy or prolactin. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
NICE takes the same line: do not routinely use postcoital testing (1.18.1); prolactin only with an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour (1.18.11); do not test for sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer hysteroscopy unless a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected (1.18.16). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ASRM also does not routinely recommend basal body temperature. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

One nuance: ASRM lists TSH among the potential routine tests in its Table 4 and mentions it mainly in oligo-anovulation, whereas NICE offers thyroid function only to people with symptoms of thyroid disease (1.18.12). [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Name four tests you would not order routinely in a basic infertility work-up.
items.application: Useful when a couple arrives with a “just in case” test list: explain which test would change management and which would not.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM 2021 (committee opinion) and NICE 2026; minor discrepancy on TSH.

items.title: Abnormal semen analysis: repeat it, and when
items.core: If the first semen analysis is abnormal, NICE offers a repeat confirmatory test, ideally 3 months later; with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, as soon as possible (1.17.3–1.17.4). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
The 3-month interval allows the cycle of sperm formation to be completed. With 2 or more abnormal analyses, NICE offers examination of the scrotum and testes and consideration of serum testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

ESHRE recommends at least one basic semen examination according to WHO criteria. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] Interpretation of the WHO manual reference values is covered in the semen analysis lesson; no figures are reproduced here.
items.recall: When would you repeat an abnormal semen analysis, and why that interval?
items.pearl: A single abnormal semen analysis is a reason to repeat, not a definitive diagnosis.

items.title: Phrase for the couple: assessing both without blame
items.core: To assess both partners without blame: NICE asks that couples be seen together because both are affected by decisions on investigation and treatment (1.1.1), and ASRM grounds simultaneous evaluation on the high prevalence of a contributing male factor. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
Suggested wording: “We are going to assess both of you at the same time. We are not looking for someone to blame: it is the most complete way to understand what is happening, and the decisions affect you both.”

NICE also recommends offering counselling because fertility problems, and their investigation and treatment, can cause psychological stress (1.2.3), and that the setting allows sensitive issues such as sexual abuse to be discussed (1.16.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: How would you explain to a couple why both partners are assessed at once?
items.application: Avoid phrases like “just relax and it will happen”: they place on the patient a responsibility that is not hers.

items.stem: Heterosexual couple; she is 33 and they have been trying for 14 months. He has a child from a previous relationship. What is appropriate regarding him?

options.text: Reproductive history and at least one semen analysis from the outset, alongside her work-up.
options.why: Correct: ASRM calls for both evaluations to start together with at least one semen analysis, and AUA/ASRM recommends concurrent assessment.

options.text: Evaluate him only if her work-up is normal.
options.why: That is sequential evaluation; guidelines recommend simultaneous assessment.

options.text: Do not evaluate him, because his fertility is already proven.
options.why: The guidelines reviewed recommend assessing both partners and make no exception for previous paternity.

options.text: Order sperm DNA fragmentation as the first test.
options.why: NICE advises against this test and ASRM excludes it from the routine work-up; the first test is a semen analysis.

items.explanation: Couple evaluation is simultaneous from the start: the male partner's reproductive history and semen analysis alongside the female work-up.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman under infertility evaluation, regular cycles, no galactorrhoea and no thyroid symptoms. Which test is NOT recommended routinely according to ASRM 2021 and NICE?

options.text: Serum prolactin.
options.why: Correct: ASRM does not recommend it routinely and NICE reserves it for an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour.

options.text: Semen analysis of her partner.
options.why: It is one of the pillars of the basic work-up.

options.text: Tubal patency test (HSG or HyCoSy).
options.why: Tubal patency is part of the basic work-up.

options.text: Detailed menstrual history.
options.why: It is the basis for assessing ovulation and, with regular cycles, is usually enough.

items.explanation: Prolactin, postcoital testing, karyotype, thrombophilia and immunological tests are not part of the routine work-up without a clinical indication.

items.stem: A woman with regular 28-day cycles and no hirsutism. Which statement about ovulation confirmation is correct?

options.text: ASRM and ESHRE do not consider it routinely necessary, whereas NICE offers mid-luteal progesterone even with regular cycles.
options.why: Correct: it is a genuine discrepancy between guidelines.

options.text: All three guidelines require mid-luteal progesterone.
options.why: Only NICE offers it with regular cycles; ASRM and ESHRE do not consider it routinely necessary.

options.text: Basal body temperature charting is the method of choice.
options.why: NICE advises against using it to confirm ovulation and ASRM does not recommend it routinely.

options.text: Endometrial biopsy with histological dating confirms ovulation.
options.why: ASRM explains that endometrial dating lacks accuracy and precision and is no longer recommended.

items.explanation: With regular cycles the menstrual history usually suffices (ASRM, ESHRE); NICE keeps mid-luteal progesterone. Knowing the discrepancy avoids presenting one practice as universal.

items.title: Female age: the main predictor of fecundity
items.core: Female fecundity decreases gradually but significantly from about age 32, and more rapidly after 37. [[ref:acog-asrm-2014-co589]]
items.body:
For ASRM, female age is the single most important predictor of fecundity. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]] Relative fertility at 40 is about half that of the late 20s and early 30s; the age-related fall in the chances of pregnancy and live birth goes with a rising risk of aneuploidy and miscarriage. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]

ACOG/ASRM add that, with age, disorders that impair fertility become more frequent and the risk of pregnancy loss rises. [[ref:acog-asrm-2014-co589]]

ASRM also notes that the chances of pregnancy and live birth decrease significantly after age 35. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]
items.recall: From which ages do ACOG/ASRM describe the decline in female fecundity?
items.pearl: Age does not only lower the chance of pregnancy: it also raises the chance of loss. That is why pregnancy and live birth must be kept apart.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ACOG/ASRM 2014 and ASRM 2021–2022 committee opinions, based on observational data. CO 589 (2014): current status not confirmed.

items.title: Age versus ovarian reserve: what each predicts
items.core: NICE advises using maternal age as the initial predictor of the overall chance of pregnancy, both through spontaneous conception and with IVF (1.18.2). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Ovarian reserve tests should augment, not replace, counselling based on age and diagnosis; low reserve does not necessarily imply inability to conceive or subfertility. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

NICE advises against using AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3) and keeps AMH and antral follicle count for predicting ovarian response and counselling on the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: To estimate the overall chance of pregnancy, what does NICE use as the initial predictor?
items.pearl: Working summary: age guides the chance of pregnancy; AMH and antral count, the response to stimulation. Details in the ovarian reserve lesson.

items.title: Paternal age: fertility and offspring health are different questions
items.core: Female fertility and, to a lesser extent, male fertility decline with age (1.4.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ASRM specifies that semen parameters decline detectably after age 35, but male fertility does not appear to be appreciably affected before about age 50. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]

Offspring health is a separate issue: the AUA/ASRM guideline advises informing couples with advanced paternal age (≥40) of an increased risk of adverse health outcomes in offspring. This is Expert Opinion, not an evidence-graded recommendation. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: What does AUA/ASRM advise for paternal age ≥40, and with what level of support?
items.application: When discussing paternal age, explicitly separate “chance of pregnancy” from “risks for offspring” so the messages are not mixed.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE 2026; ASRM 2022 (committee opinion); AUA/ASRM Statement 7: Expert Opinion.

items.title: Chance of conceiving over time
items.core: According to NICE, over 80% of heterosexual couples in the general population conceive within 1 year if the woman is under 40 and they have regular vaginal intercourse without contraception; of those who do not, about half do so in the second year (cumulative rate over 90%) (1.4.1). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
NICE's tables express clinical pregnancy, not live birth. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

ASRM adds that the likelihood of conception is highest in the first months of trying and declines gradually thereafter; fecundability (probability of pregnancy per month) is greatest in the first 3 months. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]
items.recall: What proportion of couples conceive within 1 year according to NICE, and under what conditions?
items.pearl: When quoting these figures, always name the outcome: clinical pregnancy is not the same as live birth.

items.stem: According to ACOG/ASRM (CO 589), how does female fecundity change with age?

options.text: It decreases gradually but significantly from about 32 and more rapidly after 37.
options.why: Correct: this is the wording of the CO 589 abstract.

options.text: It remains stable until 40 and then falls abruptly.
options.why: CO 589 places the start of the decline at around 32, not at 40.

options.text: It only starts to decline after 37.
options.why: At 37 it accelerates; the decline starts earlier, around 32.

options.text: It declines at the same rate as male fertility.
options.why: NICE says male fertility declines to a lesser extent, and ASRM that the effects of age are much more pronounced in women.

items.explanation: Gradual decline from ~32 and faster after 37; female age is the main predictor of fecundity.

items.stem: According to NICE NG257, what is used as the initial predictor of the overall chance of pregnancy through spontaneous conception?

options.text: Maternal age.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 1.18.2.

options.text: AMH.
options.why: NICE advises against using AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3).

options.text: Basal FSH.
options.why: NICE advises against FSH even as a predictor of response or outcome in assisted conception (1.18.5), and ASRM notes that reserve tests in women without infertility do not predict short-term fecundity.

options.text: Antral follicle count.
options.why: NICE uses it to predict ovarian response in assisted conception (1.18.4), not spontaneous pregnancy.

items.explanation: Age guides the chance of pregnancy; reserve markers guide the response to stimulation.

items.stem: Regarding advanced paternal age (≥40), what does the AUA/ASRM male infertility guideline state?

options.text: It advises informing the couple of an increased risk of adverse health outcomes in offspring; it is Expert Opinion.
options.why: Correct: Statement 7, labelled Expert Opinion.

options.text: The same, but as a strong recommendation with Grade A evidence.
options.why: The content is right but the grading is not: it is Expert Opinion.

options.text: It recommends postponing conception until genetic testing is completed.
options.why: Statement 7 is about informing on risk, not postponing conception or genetic testing.

options.text: It states that male fertility falls appreciably from age 35.
options.why: According to ASRM, semen parameters decline after 35 but fertility does not appear appreciably affected before ~50.

items.explanation: Separate a recommendation's content from its support: here the message is reasonable but rests on expert opinion.

items.title: What I would do: when to start evaluation by age
items.core: Absent findings that demand earlier action, ASRM advises starting evaluation at 12 months if the woman is under 35 and at 6 months if she is 35 or older; over 40, more immediate evaluation and treatment may be warranted. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]
items.body:
Evaluation starts without delay if there is a known condition that causes infertility: irregular cycles or cycles shorter than 25 days, intermenstrual bleeding, oligo- or amenorrhoea; known or suspected uterine, tubal or peritoneal disease or endometriosis; known or suspected male subfertility; sexual dysfunction; or conditions predisposing to diminished ovarian reserve (e.g., chemotherapy, radiation, FMR1 premutation). [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

ACOG/ASRM (CO 589) put it this way: in women older than 35, expedited evaluation and treatment after 6 months of failed attempts, or earlier if clinically indicated; over 40, more immediate evaluation and treatment. [[ref:acog-asrm-2014-co589]]
items.recall: After how many months of trying does evaluation start at <35, ≥35 and >40 years according to ASRM?

rows.text: >40 years: more immediate evaluation and treatment

visual.alt: Flow diagram (ASRM 2021): if there is a known condition causing infertility, evaluate without delay; otherwise by the woman's age: under 35 at 12 months, 35 or older at 6 months, over 40 more immediately.

items.application: At 35 or older, the visit at 6 months is already the time to evaluate, not to “wait for the full year”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM 2021 and ACOG/ASRM 2014 (committee opinions; no formal evidence grading).

items.title: ASRM versus NICE: two age thresholds
items.core: NICE offers referral for a specialist consultation at presentation if the person trying to become pregnant is 36 or over, or if either partner has a known or suspected clinical cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Outside those situations, NICE offers both partners assessment after 1 year of unprotected vaginal intercourse (1.16.5) or after 6 cycles of artificial insemination (1.16.6). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ASRM uses a different cut-off: evaluation at 6 months from age 35. [[ref:asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation]]

NICE's list of suspected causes includes, among others: irregular or absent periods, significant pelvic pain, endometriosis or chronic PID, previous ectopic pregnancy, recurrent ovarian cystectomies, multiple abdominopelvic surgeries, and in men undescended testes, testicular cancer, clinically significant varicocele or post-pubertal orchitis. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: From what age does NICE offer referral at the first consultation?
items.pearl: Different thresholds, same logic: the older the woman, the shorter the wait before evaluation. NICE also reflects how the UK health system is organised.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE 2026 (UK national guideline); ASRM 2021 (US committee opinion).

items.title: A miscarriage while trying does not reset the clock
items.core: If a miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy occurs during the year of trying before investigation, NICE advises continuing the timeframe rather than restarting it (1.16.7). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
The same rule applies to the period of expectant management in unexplained infertility and to the 12 cycles of artificial insemination before IVF access (different from the 6 cycles in 1.16.6 before investigation). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Nuance: NICE's glossary lists a history of ectopic pregnancy among suspected clinical causes, which justify offering referral at presentation (1.16.8); the NICE text does not detail how to combine both recommendations. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: After a miscarriage in month 7 of trying, does the 1-year timeframe restart according to NICE?
items.application: Avoids the disheartening message of “starting from zero” after a loss.

items.title: While trying: what to advise about the fertile window
items.core: The fertile window spans the 6 days ending on the day of ovulation; intercourse every 1–2 days within that window yields the highest pregnancy rates, and 2–3 times per week gives nearly equivalent results. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]
items.body:
Couples should not be advised to limit the frequency of intercourse. Fertility-awareness methods, such as ovulation kits or cervical mucus monitoring, are associated with a higher probability of conceiving in a given cycle but can cause stress; if used, they should guide frequent intercourse, not replace it. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]] NICE informs that vaginal intercourse every 2–3 days optimises the chance of pregnancy (1.5.1). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Coital position and postcoital routines have no impact on fertility, and there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility; women attempting to conceive should be advised to take a folic acid supplement (at least 400 µg daily) to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]
items.recall: How does ASRM define the fertile window, and what intercourse frequency does it advise?
items.pearl: ASRM leaves the exact frequency to the couple's preference within the fertile window: a rigid schedule can add stress without benefit.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ASRM 2022 (consensus-based committee opinion; mostly observational data); NICE 2026.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman, regular cycles, no relevant history; she has been trying to conceive with her partner for 7 months. According to ASRM, what is appropriate?

options.text: Start evaluation of both partners now.
options.why: Correct: from age 35, evaluation starts at 6 months and includes both partners.

options.text: Wait until 12 months of trying are completed.
options.why: The 12-month threshold applies to women under 35.

options.text: Order only an AMH to decide whether they can keep waiting.
options.why: A lone AMH does not replace the evaluation: ASRM sees it as an adjunct to the evaluation of the infertile woman, and notes that low reserve does not necessarily imply inability to conceive.

options.text: Go straight to IVF without prior work-up.
options.why: Systematic evaluation aims to identify all relevant factors before deciding on treatment.

items.explanation: At 35 or older, 6 months without pregnancy is enough to start evaluating both partners; over 40, even more immediately.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman with no known cause of infertility presents after 3 months of trying. According to NICE NG257, what is appropriate?

options.text: Offer referral for a specialist consultation at this first visit.
options.why: Correct: NICE offers it at presentation from age 36 (1.16.8).

options.text: Wait until 1 year of unprotected intercourse is completed.
options.why: That timeframe applies when the woman is under 36 and there is no known cause or predisposing factor.

options.text: Wait until 6 months are completed.
options.why: That is the ASRM threshold for women aged 35 or over, not NICE's.

options.text: Refer only if AMH is low.
options.why: NICE advises against using AMH to predict spontaneous pregnancy (1.18.3); referral depends on age and causes.

items.explanation: NICE: referral at presentation at 36 or over, or with a known cause or predisposing factors in either partner.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with no known cause of infertility had a miscarriage in month 7 of trying. According to NICE, how is the timeframe for investigation counted?

options.text: It continues from the start of trying, without restarting.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 1.16.7.

options.text: It restarts: another 12 months from the miscarriage.
options.why: NICE explicitly advises not restarting the timeframe.

options.text: It is paused for 6 months and then resumed.
options.why: NICE does not include such a pause; the timeframe continues.

options.text: The miscarriage mandates immediate referral.
options.why: A single miscarriage is not among NICE criteria for referral at presentation (age ≥36 or a known or suspected cause); NICE advises continuing the timeframe.

items.explanation: A loss while trying does not restart the 1-year timeframe; saying so avoids delays and discouragement.

items.stem: A couple with no evidence of infertility asks how to plan intercourse. Which advice agrees with ASRM 2022?

options.text: Intercourse every 1–2 days in the fertile window, although 2–3 times per week gives nearly equivalent results; no need to limit frequency.
options.why: Correct: this is the ASRM summary.

options.text: Space intercourse every 4–5 days to “concentrate” the semen.
options.why: ASRM notes that believing frequent ejaculation reduces fertility is a misconception and advises not limiting frequency.

options.text: A single act of intercourse on the day of a positive LH test.
options.why: In the data cited by ASRM, cycle fecundity was lowest with intercourse only once in the fertile window.

options.text: Lie supine after intercourse to improve sperm transport.
options.why: ASRM states this belief has no scientific foundation.

items.explanation: A 6-day fertile window, frequent intercourse without a rigid schedule, and no postcoital rituals.

items.stem: In the AUA/ASRM male infertility guideline, how are these two statements graded: concurrent assessment of both partners, and one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation?

options.text: Both: Strong Recommendation, Grade A.
options.why: Neither is Grade A: concurrent assessment is Expert Opinion and semen analysis is Strong, Grade B.

options.text: Concurrent assessment: Strong Recommendation, Grade B; semen analysis: Expert Opinion.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: Concurrent assessment: Expert Opinion; semen analysis: Strong Recommendation, Grade B.
options.why: Correct: that is how they appear in the AUA/ASRM guideline.

options.text: Both: Expert Opinion.
options.why: Semen analysis in the initial evaluation is a Strong Recommendation with Grade B evidence.

items.explanation: AUA/ASRM: concurrent assessment of both partners = Expert Opinion; one or more semen analyses in the initial evaluation = Strong Recommendation, Grade B. ASRM 2021 grounds it on the high prevalence of a contributing male factor.

items.stem: A 34-year-old single woman planning pregnancy with donor sperm consults because she has not conceived. According to ASRM 2021, how should she be evaluated?

options.text: With a directed history, examination and laboratory evaluation as for any infertile patient, tailoring tubal and uterine assessment to her history and risk.
options.why: Correct: that is ASRM’s advice for people who need donor sperm.

options.text: She needs no evaluation, because there is no male factor to study.
options.why: ASRM advises evaluating her as any infertile patient.

options.text: Only with an AMH to decide whether to keep trying.
options.why: AMH does not predict spontaneous conception and does not replace a directed evaluation.

options.text: With routine laparoscopy, because no semen analysis can be done.
options.why: ASRM does not recommend routine laparoscopy without suspected pelvic pathology or another indication.

items.explanation: With donor sperm (single women, female couples), ASRM advises a directed evaluation as for any infertile patient, tailoring tubal and uterine assessment to history and risk.

items.stem: According to ASRM 2021, which is the best imaging modality to assess uterine anatomy in the basic work-up?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy.
options.why: It is not a routine imaging test: ASRM does not recommend it without suspected pelvic pathology or another indication.

options.text: Endometrial biopsy.
options.why: It is not an imaging test and is not part of the routine work-up without an indication.

options.text: Hysterosalpingography as the only uterine test.
options.why: ASRM recommends HSG (or sonohysterography) for tubal patency; for uterine anatomy it prefers transvaginal ultrasound.

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound.
options.why: Correct: ASRM considers it the best modality for uterine anatomy.

items.explanation: Pillars of the basic work-up: ovulatory status, structure and patency of the female tract, and semen analysis. For the uterus, transvaginal ultrasound; for the tubes, HSG or sonohysterography.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy or endometriosis. According to NICE, which test is offered to assess tubal patency?

options.text: Laparoscopy and dye.
options.why: NICE reserves it for people thought to have comorbidities such as PID, previous ectopic pregnancy or endometriosis.

options.text: Hysterosalpingography (HSG).
options.why: Correct: NICE offers it to people without known comorbidities (1.18.13).

options.text: Hysteroscopy.
options.why: NICE does not offer it unless a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected, and it does not assess tubal patency.

options.text: None: tubal patency is not part of the basic work-up.
options.why: Structure and patency of the reproductive tract is one of the three pillars of the basic work-up.

items.explanation: NICE: HSG without known comorbidities (1.18.13); laparoscopy and dye if they are suspected (1.18.15). ESHRE considers HSG and HyCoSy valid (strong; ⊕⊕⊕○).

items.stem: A woman with regular 32-day cycles. If you decide to measure progesterone to confirm ovulation, when should it be done according to ASRM?

options.text: On day 21, as in any cycle.
options.why: ASRM advises against a fixed day such as day 21: in a 32-day cycle it would be too early.

options.text: On day 14, at the time of ovulation.
options.why: Progesterone is measured in the luteal phase, about 1 week before menses.

options.text: Around day 25, about 1 week before the expected period.
options.why: Correct: it is timed to the next expected period.

options.text: On three consecutive luteal days, to assess luteal quality.
options.why: One value confirms ovulation, but ASRM notes it does not assess luteal phase quality.

items.explanation: ASRM: progesterone about 1 week before the expected period (in a 32-day cycle, around day 25), not on a fixed day. It confirms ovulation; it does not judge luteal “quality”.

items.stem: A patient with regular cycles asks whether she should chart her basal body temperature to confirm ovulation. What do the guidelines say?

options.text: NICE advises against using basal body temperature charts to confirm ovulation and ASRM does not recommend it routinely.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.18.9 and ASRM 2021.

options.text: It is the method of choice according to ESHRE.
options.why: ESHRE does not propose it; if confirmation is warranted, it states that tests such as urinary LH can be used.

options.text: NICE prefers it to mid-luteal progesterone.
options.why: The opposite: NICE offers mid-luteal progesterone and advises against basal body temperature.

options.text: It is essential before any other test.
options.why: None of the guidelines requires it; NICE states it does not reliably predict ovulation.

items.explanation: With regular cycles, ASRM and ESHRE do not consider routine ovulation confirmation necessary; NICE offers mid-luteal progesterone. On basal body temperature: NICE advises against using it to confirm ovulation, ASRM does not recommend it routinely, and ESHRE does not include it among the tests it lists, given its lower accuracy.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman under infertility evaluation, with no symptoms of thyroid disease. How do ASRM 2021 and NICE 2026 differ on TSH?

options.text: Both order TSH for all women under evaluation.
options.why: NICE offers it only with symptoms of thyroid disease.

options.text: NICE orders it routinely; ASRM only with symptoms.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: Neither mentions thyroid function.
options.why: Both address it, with different criteria.

options.text: ASRM lists TSH among potential routine tests; NICE offers thyroid function only if there are symptoms of thyroid disease.
options.why: Correct: it is a genuine nuance between the two guidelines (NICE 1.18.12).

items.explanation: On the “do not order routinely” list ASRM and NICE agree on almost everything; the nuance is TSH: a potential routine test for ASRM, only with symptoms for NICE.

items.stem: A couple arrives with a “just in case” test list: karyotype, thrombophilia testing, postcoital test and semen analysis. Without other indications, which one belongs to the basic work-up?

options.text: Karyotype.
options.why: ASRM does not recommend it routinely without a clinical indication.

options.text: Semen analysis.
options.why: Correct: it is one of the three pillars of the basic work-up.

options.text: Thrombophilia testing.
options.why: ASRM does not recommend it routinely without a clinical indication.

options.text: Postcoital test.
options.why: Neither ASRM nor NICE recommends it routinely (NICE 1.18.1).

items.explanation: Explain which test would change management: semen analysis does; karyotype, thrombophilia, immunological testing, postcoital test, endometrial biopsy or laparoscopy do not, routinely, without an indication.

items.stem: According to NICE 2026, when is hysteroscopy offered in the infertility work-up?

options.text: Routinely to all women before IVF.
options.why: NICE does not offer it routinely.

options.text: After a single abnormal semen analysis.
options.why: An abnormal semen analysis leads to a repeat test, not to hysteroscopy.

options.text: Only if a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.18.16.

options.text: Whenever AMH is low.
options.why: AMH is not an indication for hysteroscopy; its use is to predict ovarian response.

items.explanation: NICE: do not offer hysteroscopy unless a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected (1.18.16); nor routine postcoital testing or sperm DNA fragmentation.

items.stem: A man’s first semen analysis is abnormal, without azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia. According to NICE, what is appropriate?

options.text: Repeat it, ideally 3 months later.
options.why: Correct: the interval allows the cycle of sperm formation to be completed.

options.text: Treat it as a definitive diagnosis.
options.why: A single abnormal semen analysis is a reason to repeat, not a definitive diagnosis.

options.text: Order sperm DNA fragmentation.
options.why: NICE advises against that test (1.17.6).

options.text: Repeat it the following week.
options.why: Immediate repetition is reserved for azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia.

items.explanation: NICE 1.17.3–1.17.4: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally after 3 months; sooner if there is azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia.

items.stem: The first semen analysis shows azoospermia. According to NICE, when is it repeated?

options.text: At 3 months, like any abnormal semen analysis.
options.why: With a gross deficiency (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia), NICE says not to wait.

options.text: It is not repeated: azoospermia needs no confirmation.
options.why: NICE offers a confirmatory test in this case too, but without delay.

options.text: Only once the woman’s work-up is complete.
options.why: Both partners are evaluated at the same time; you do not wait for her work-up.

options.text: As soon as possible.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.17.4.

items.explanation: The 3-month wait aims to complete the sperm formation cycle; with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, confirmation is done as soon as possible.

items.stem: A man has 2 abnormal semen analyses. According to NICE 2026, what is offered next?

options.text: A sperm DNA fragmentation test.
options.why: NICE advises against that test (1.17.6).

options.text: Physical examination of the scrotum and testes, and consideration of serum testosterone and gonadotrophins.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.17.5.

options.text: A third semen analysis with no further assessment.
options.why: After 2 or more abnormal results, NICE moves on to examination and hormonal assessment.

options.text: No further male evaluation; straight to IVF.
options.why: NICE offers clinical assessment of the man before deciding.

items.explanation: NICE: with 2 or more abnormal semen analyses, examine the scrotum and testes and consider testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5). Interpreting WHO reference values is covered in another lesson.

items.stem: First visit of a couple who have been trying for 14 months. Which phrase best conveys a blame-free evaluation?

options.text: “Just relax and it will happen.”
options.why: It places on the patient a responsibility that is not hers; it is exactly what to avoid.

options.text: “We’ll start with you and, if everything is normal, we’ll assess your partner.”
options.why: Evaluation of both should start at the same time, given the high prevalence of a contributing male factor.

options.text: “We are going to assess both of you at the same time: we are not looking for someone to blame; it is the most complete way to understand what is happening, and the decisions affect you both.”
options.why: Correct: simultaneous, blame-free evaluation.

options.text: “Since he already has a child, the problem must be with you.”
options.why: It assigns blame and presumes the cause; both are evaluated simultaneously.

items.explanation: NICE asks to see the couple together because decisions affect both (1.1.1), and ASRM grounds simultaneous evaluation on how common the male factor is.

items.stem: According to NICE, why and when is counselling offered to people with fertility problems?

options.text: Because fertility problems, and also their investigation and treatment, can cause psychological stress; it is offered before, during and after, whatever the outcome.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.2.3–1.2.4.

options.text: Only if treatment fails, because that is when stress appears.
options.why: NICE offers it before, during and after investigation and treatment, whatever the outcome.

options.text: Only to the woman, because she undergoes more tests.
options.why: NICE offers it to people with fertility problems and recommends seeing the couple together.

options.text: Only once IVF is reached.
options.why: Support is offered from the investigation stage, not only at IVF.

items.explanation: NICE: offer counselling because the problem and its investigation and treatment cause stress (1.2.3), before, during and after, whatever the outcome (1.2.4); and a setting that allows sensitive issues such as sexual abuse to be discussed (1.16.3).

items.stem: According to ASRM 2022, roughly how does relative fertility at 40 compare with that of the late 20s and early 30s?

options.text: Practically the same.
options.why: At 40, relative fertility is already about half that of the late 20s and early 30s, according to ASRM 2022.

options.text: About 90%.
options.why: It underestimates the decline: ASRM puts it at about half.

options.text: Zero: at 40 there is no natural fertility.
options.why: It is a major decline, not a disappearance: about half.

options.text: About half.
options.why: Correct: that is the figure ASRM reports.

items.explanation: Female age is the most important predictor of fecundity: at 40, relative fertility is about half, and aneuploidy and miscarriage increase.

items.stem: When counselling a 41-year-old woman, why should “pregnancy” and “live birth” be kept apart?

options.text: Because age only affects the chance of pregnancy, not its course.
options.why: Age also increases the risk of pregnancy loss.

options.text: Because with age the chance of pregnancy falls and, in addition, the risk of aneuploidy and miscarriage rises.
options.why: Correct: age acts at both ends.

options.text: Because after 40 the risk of miscarriage decreases.
options.why: The opposite occurs: it increases.

options.text: Because it is a distinction relevant only to IVF.
options.why: It also applies to spontaneous conception: the decline affects both pregnancy and live birth.

items.explanation: ASRM: the age-related fall in the chance of pregnancy and live birth comes with more aneuploidy and miscarriage; ACOG/ASRM add that disorders that impair fertility become more frequent.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman, regular cycles, with a low AMH and no diagnosed infertility, asks whether she can conceive spontaneously. What is most accurate according to ASRM 2021?

options.text: Low reserve means she will not conceive without treatment.
options.why: ASRM notes that low reserve does not necessarily imply inability to conceive or subfertility.

options.text: AMH predicts her chance of spontaneous pregnancy better than age.
options.why: NICE uses age as the initial predictor and advises against AMH to predict spontaneous pregnancy.

options.text: Reserve tests augment, rather than replace, counselling based on age and diagnosis; low reserve does not necessarily imply subfertility.
options.why: Correct: that is ASRM’s position.

options.text: She should repeat the AMH every 3 months to monitor her fertility.
options.why: AMH is not a test to predict spontaneous pregnancy; repeating it does not change that.

items.explanation: Age guides the chance of pregnancy; AMH and antral count, the response to stimulation. Reserve tests augment counselling based on age and diagnosis.

items.stem: According to NICE 2026, which pairing of predictor and use is correct?

options.text: Age: overall chance of pregnancy, spontaneous and with IVF. AMH or AFC: ovarian response and counselling on live birth after assisted conception.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.18.2 and 1.18.4.

options.text: AMH: chance of spontaneous pregnancy. Age: ovarian response.
options.why: NICE advises against AMH to predict spontaneous pregnancy (1.18.3).

options.text: FSH: ovarian response. AMH: spontaneous pregnancy.
options.why: NICE advises against FSH as a response predictor and against AMH for spontaneous pregnancy.

options.text: AFC: overall chance of spontaneous pregnancy. Age: not used as a predictor.
options.why: Age is precisely the initial predictor of the overall chance of pregnancy.

items.explanation: NICE: maternal age is the initial predictor of the overall chance of pregnancy (1.18.2); AMH/AFC predict response and help counsel on live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4); AMH does not predict spontaneous pregnancy (1.18.3).

items.stem: A 45-year-old man whose partner is 32 asks whether his age reduces the chance of pregnancy. According to ASRM 2022, what is most accurate?

options.text: His fertility is already half of what it was at 30.
options.why: That figure refers to female fertility at 40, not male fertility.

options.text: Male age has no influence at all, neither on semen nor on offspring.
options.why: Semen changes after 35 and, separately, AUA/ASRM advises informing about offspring risk from 40.

options.text: Male fertility declines just like female fertility.
options.why: NICE states that male fertility declines to a lesser extent.

options.text: Semen parameters decline detectably after 35, but male fertility does not appear appreciably affected before about 50.
options.why: Correct: that is what ASRM specifies.

items.explanation: Separate two questions: chance of pregnancy (little affected before about 50 per ASRM) and offspring health (AUA/ASRM: inform of increased risk at ≥40; Expert Opinion).

items.stem: According to NICE 2026 (1.4.3), how does age affect fertility?

options.text: Only female fertility declines.
options.why: NICE also includes male fertility, though to a lesser extent.

options.text: Female fertility and, to a lesser extent, male fertility decline.
options.why: Correct: that is how NICE phrases it.

options.text: Both decline to the same extent.
options.why: NICE states that male fertility declines to a lesser extent.

options.text: Mainly male fertility declines.
options.why: It is the other way round: the main effect is on female fertility.

items.explanation: NICE 1.4.3: female fertility and, to a lesser extent, male fertility decline with age.

items.stem: A heterosexual couple from the general population (woman under 40), regular intercourse without contraception, not pregnant after 1 year. According to NICE, what proportion of such couples conceive in the second year?

options.text: About 10%.
options.why: Underestimate: NICE states that about half conceive in the second year.

options.text: Over 80%.
options.why: Over 80% is the proportion that conceives in the first year.

options.text: About half.
options.why: Correct: that is how the cumulative rate exceeds 90%.

options.text: Practically none without treatment.
options.why: NICE states that about half conceive in the second year.

items.explanation: NICE 1.4.1: over 80% conceive within 1 year; of those who do not, about half do in the second (cumulative >90%). These are clinical pregnancy figures, not live birth.

items.stem: According to ASRM 2022, when is fecundability (probability of pregnancy per month) highest?

options.text: In the first 3 months of trying.
options.why: Correct: it then declines gradually.

options.text: Between months 6 and 12.
options.why: The probability is highest at the beginning and then falls.

options.text: It is constant during the first year.
options.why: It is not constant: it is highest at the beginning and declines gradually.

options.text: It increases with each passing month.
options.why: The opposite occurs: it declines gradually.

items.explanation: The likelihood of conception is highest in the first months and then declines; fecundability is greatest in the first 3 months.

items.stem: When quoting NICE’s tables on the cumulative probability of conceiving, which outcome do they express?

options.text: Live birth.
options.why: NICE’s tables express clinical pregnancy, not live birth.

options.text: Ongoing pregnancy at 12 weeks.
options.why: That is not the outcome of those tables: they express clinical pregnancy.

options.text: Positive urine pregnancy test.
options.why: No: the outcome is clinical pregnancy.

options.text: Clinical pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: which is why you should always name the outcome.

items.explanation: Clinical pregnancy is not the same as live birth: when quoting figures, always name the outcome.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with 22-day cycles has been trying for 4 months. According to ASRM 2021, what is appropriate?

options.text: Wait until 12 months, because she is under 35.
options.why: Cycles shorter than 25 days are a condition that justifies evaluation without delay.

options.text: Start evaluation without delay.
options.why: Correct: cycles shorter than 25 days are on ASRM’s list for not waiting.

options.text: Wait until 6 months.
options.why: The 6-month threshold is for women aged 35 or more without other findings; here there is a reason to evaluate now.

options.text: Order only an AMH to decide whether she can keep waiting.
options.why: AMH does not indicate whether one can wait; the evaluation should start.

items.explanation: ASRM: evaluate without delay with irregular cycles or cycles shorter than 25 days, intermenstrual bleeding, oligo/amenorrhoea, suspected uterine, tubal or peritoneal disease or endometriosis, known or suspected male subfertility, sexual dysfunction or conditions predisposing to diminished reserve.

items.stem: Which of these situations is, according to ASRM 2021, a reason to evaluate without waiting 6–12 months?

options.text: A 30-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles, trying for 3 months.
options.why: There is no finding from ASRM’s list; under 35, evaluation is at 12 months.

options.text: Male partner with a child from a previous relationship.
options.why: It is not among ASRM’s conditions for earlier evaluation; besides, he is evaluated from the outset anyway.

options.text: Previous chemotherapy.
options.why: Correct: it is a condition predisposing to diminished ovarian reserve.

options.text: Wish to know the AMH before trying.
options.why: It is not an indication for infertility evaluation; AMH does not predict spontaneous conception.

items.explanation: Conditions predisposing to diminished reserve (chemotherapy, radiation, FMR1 premutation) justify evaluation without waiting; over 40, more immediate evaluation and treatment.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman, with no known cause or predisposing factors, has been trying for 4 months. What do ASRM and NICE recommend?

options.text: ASRM: evaluate at 6 months of trying. NICE: assessment of both after 1 year, because referral at presentation applies from 36.
options.why: Correct: two different thresholds for the same logic.

options.text: Both: immediate referral because of age.
options.why: NICE offers referral at presentation from 36; ASRM evaluates at 6 months from 35.

options.text: ASRM: wait 12 months. NICE: refer now.
options.why: It is reversed: ASRM shortens to 6 months from 35, and NICE refers at presentation from 36.

options.text: Both: wait 12 months.
options.why: ASRM evaluates at 6 months from age 35.

items.explanation: Different thresholds, same logic: ASRM, 6 months from 35; NICE, referral at presentation from 36 or with a suspected cause, and otherwise assessment after 1 year.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a female partner is trying to conceive with donor-sperm artificial insemination; no known cause of infertility. According to NICE, when is clinical assessment offered?

options.text: After 12 insemination cycles.
options.why: The 12 cycles relate to IVF access, not to assessment (which is at 6).

options.text: After 1 year of trying, as with intercourse.
options.why: The 1-year timeframe applies to unprotected vaginal intercourse; with insemination, NICE uses 6 cycles.

options.text: At presentation, always.
options.why: Referral at presentation is for age 36 or over, or with a known or suspected cause.

options.text: After 6 insemination cycles without pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.16.6.

items.explanation: NICE: assessment after 1 year of unprotected vaginal intercourse (1.16.5) or after 6 cycles of artificial insemination (1.16.6), unless there is a reason to refer at presentation (1.16.8).

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman, with no known cause, had an ectopic pregnancy at month 5 of trying. Which statement about NICE is correct?

options.text: The timeframe restarts: another 12 months from the ectopic.
options.why: NICE says to continue the timeframe without restarting it after a miscarriage or ectopic (1.16.7).

options.text: The timeframe continues without restarting (1.16.7); in addition, NICE’s glossary lists a history of ectopic pregnancy among the suspected clinical causes that justify offering referral at presentation (1.16.8), and the guideline text does not detail how the two recommendations combine.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.16.7 says to continue the timeframe, and its glossary lists previous ectopic among the suspected causes in 1.16.8; the text does not detail how to combine them.

options.text: The ectopic is not taken into account in any NICE recommendation.
options.why: It appears both in the rule of not restarting the timeframe and in the glossary of suspected causes.

options.text: The timeframe is paused for 6 months and then resumed.
options.why: NICE does not provide for pauses: the timeframe continues.

items.explanation: NICE 1.16.7 (2026): after a miscarriage or ectopic, continue the timeframe. Separately, a previous ectopic is among the suspected causes in 1.16.8; the guideline text does not detail how to combine them.

items.stem: A woman undergoing artificial insemination has a miscarriage after the eighth cycle. According to NICE, how are the 12 insemination cycles counted?

options.text: They restart from zero.
options.why: NICE says not to restart the timeframe after a miscarriage or ectopic.

options.text: Only the cycles after the miscarriage are counted, up to 6.
options.why: No: the timeframe continues without restarting.

options.text: They continue from the eighth cycle.
options.why: Correct: the rule in 1.16.7 includes the 12 insemination cycles.

options.text: The rule applies only to intercourse, not to insemination.
options.why: NICE also applies it to the expectant management period and to the 12 insemination cycles.

items.explanation: NICE 1.16.7 applies to the year of unprotected intercourse, to the expectant management period in unexplained infertility and to the 12 cycles of artificial insemination.

items.stem: According to ASRM 2022, how is the fertile window best defined?

options.text: The 6 days ending on the day of ovulation.
options.why: Correct: that is ASRM’s definition.

options.text: The 6 days after ovulation.
options.why: The window ends on the day of ovulation; it does not extend afterwards.

options.text: The middle 14 days of the cycle.
options.why: ASRM defines it as 6 days ending on the day of ovulation.

options.text: Only the day of the LH surge.
options.why: It is wider: 6 days ending on the day of ovulation.

items.explanation: Fertile window: 6 days ending on the day of ovulation. Intercourse every 1–2 days within it gives the highest rates; 2–3 times per week, nearly equivalent results.

items.stem: A couple uses ovulation kits and only has intercourse on the day of a positive test; trying is causing them a lot of stress. What would you advise according to ASRM 2022?

options.text: Keep going: a single well-timed act of intercourse is optimal.
options.why: The highest rates come with intercourse every 1–2 days within the fertile window.

options.text: Space intercourse to “concentrate” the semen.
options.why: ASRM states couples should not be advised to limit frequency.

options.text: Add a specific fertility diet, which improves natural fertility.
options.why: ASRM notes there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.

options.text: If they use fertility-awareness methods, these should guide frequent intercourse in the fertile window, not replace it; there is no need to limit frequency.
options.why: Correct: that is ASRM’s approach, which also warns about the stress they can cause.

items.explanation: Fertility-awareness methods are associated with a higher chance of conceiving per cycle but can cause stress; they should guide frequent intercourse, not replace it. NICE: intercourse every 2–3 days optimises the chance.

items.stem: While trying to conceive, a patient asks which dietary measure has clear evidence. What do you tell her according to ASRM 2022?

options.text: A specific “fertility” diet improves natural fertility.
options.why: ASRM states there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.

options.text: A folic acid supplement (at least 400 µg daily) is advised to reduce the risk of neural tube defects; there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.
options.why: Correct: that is ASRM’s summary.

options.text: Folic acid improves the monthly chance of conceiving.
options.why: Its documented benefit is reducing neural tube defects, not increasing fecundability.

options.text: No measure has evidence, not even folic acid.
options.why: Daily folic acid does reduce the risk of neural tube defects.

items.explanation: ASRM 2022: coital position and postcoital routines have no impact; there is insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility; daily folic acid reduces neural tube defects.

items.title: Case: Marta, Daniel and “it's still early”

steps.text: Marta (fictional case), 37, no previous pregnancies, regular 27–30-day cycles, no hirsutism. Her partner, Daniel, is 41 and has a child from a previous relationship. They have been trying for 7 months. She asks whether “it's still early”; he remarks that, since he has already fathered a child, “the problem won't be his”.
Timing: at 37 with 7 months of trying, evaluation is already due. ASRM indicates it at 6 months from age 35; NICE would offer specialist referral at presentation from age 36.

Both at once: ASRM and AUA/ASRM recommend evaluating both partners simultaneously; for this couple that means Daniel's reproductive history and at least one semen analysis from the outset, even though he has already fathered a child.

Marta's work-up: with regular cycles and no hirsutism, the menstrual history guides ovulation assessment (ASRM); transvaginal ultrasound for the uterus and HSG or HyCoSy for tubal patency. Without galactorrhoea or an ovulatory disorder, prolactin is not ordered routinely.

Paternal age: at 41, the AUA/ASRM guideline advises informing them of an increased risk of adverse health outcomes in offspring (Expert Opinion). Present it as information for the couple, separate from the question of the chance of pregnancy.

Twist: Daniel's semen analysis is reported as abnormal by his laboratory. NICE offers a repeat, ideally after 3 months (sooner with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia); meanwhile, Marta's evaluation continues in parallel.
Communication: explain that both are assessed to understand, not to assign blame, and offer psychological support, since the work-up itself can cause stress (NICE).

acog-asrm-2014-co589.title: Female age-related fertility decline. Committee Opinion No. 589
acog-asrm-2014-co589.authors: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists Committee on Gynecologic Practice; Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
acog-asrm-2014-co589.population: Women who desire pregnancy; Fertil Steril 2014;101(3):633–4.
acog-asrm-2014-co589.finding: Female fecundity decreases gradually but significantly beginning at approximately 32 years and more rapidly after 37. Women older than 35 should receive an expedited evaluation and undergo treatment after 6 months of failed attempts to conceive, or earlier if clinically indicated; in women older than 40, more immediate evaluation and treatment are warranted.
acog-asrm-2014-co589.limitations: Only the abstract was verified (PubMed). 2014 document; its current status (reaffirmation or withdrawal) could not be confirmed: the ACOG page was not accessible and the ASRM page does not list it.

asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.title: Fertility evaluation of infertile women: a committee opinion
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.population: Women evaluated for infertility (including single women, same-sex couples, transgender men and non-binary patients seeking treatment); Fertil Steril 2021;116:1255–65.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.finding: Evaluation at 12 months if <35 and at 6 months if ≥35; more immediate if >40; without delay with a known condition causing infertility. Evaluate both partners at the same time, with at least one semen analysis at onset. Basic work-up: ovulation, structure and patency of the reproductive tract, and semen analysis. With regular 21–35-day cycles, ovulation confirmation is not required (unless hirsutism). Female age is the single most important predictor of fecundity. Laparoscopy, postcoital test, thrombophilia, immunological tests, karyotype, endometrial biopsy, advanced sperm function testing and prolactin are not routine. Menstrual history may suffice to establish an ovulatory pattern; oligo/amenorrhoea establishes anovulation without further ovulation testing. If history is indeterminate: luteal progesterone (≈1 week before expected menses, not a fixed day such as day 21; >3 ng/mL = presumptive evidence of recent ovulation; a single value confirms ovulation, not luteal quality), urinary LH kits (false positives in PCOS) or transvaginal ultrasound. Basal body temperature and endometrial biopsy are not routinely recommended. Prolactin not routine; indicated with galactorrhoea or oligo/amenorrhoea.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion, not a GRADE guideline; US context; no formal strength or certainty grading.

asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.title: Optimizing natural fertility: a committee opinion
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine; Practice Committee of the Society for Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.population: Couples or individuals attempting conception with no evidence of infertility; Fertil Steril 2022;117:53–63.
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.finding: Monthly fecundability greatest in the first 3 months; relative fertility at 40 about half that of the late 20s/early 30s; semen parameters decline after 35, but male fertility does not appear appreciably affected before ~50. Fertile window: 6 days ending on the day of ovulation; intercourse every 1–2 days gives the highest rates and 2–3 times per week nearly equivalent; do not limit frequency. Position and postcoital routines have no impact; insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion based on expert consensus; most lifestyle data are observational; US context.

aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: AUA/ASRM Guideline (2020; amended 2024)
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.authors: American Urological Association; American Society for Reproductive Medicine (Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.)
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.population: Male partners of couples with infertility.
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.finding: Statement 1: concurrent assessment of both partners in the initial evaluation (Expert Opinion). Statement 2: reproductive history (Clinical Principle) and one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level Grade B). Statement 7: advise couples with advanced paternal age (≥40) of an increased risk of adverse health outcomes for offspring (Expert Opinion).
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.limitations: Official AUA page read: summary of all guideline statements and discussion on semen analysis, hormones, DNA fragmentation, pregnancy loss, imaging, varicocele, testosterone and supplements. Statement numbers do not always appear in the extracted text; Part I/II DOIs not verified. US context.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty). ICSI not recommended over conventional IVF (rec. 42, strong, ⊕); endometrial scratching should not be offered (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕); adjunct oral antioxidants in women probably not recommended (rec. 46, conditional, ⊕).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
